description: We are a team passionate about space exploration, engineering, and technology. We aim to create an intuitive tool that helps users explore lunar landing sites and understand key mission conditions. By combining programming, data analysis, and space science, we hope to turn complex lunar data into useful insights for future mission planning.
summary:
When presented with the opportunity of becoming an astronaut, the excitement is unmatched. Nothing compares to being freed from the boundaries of Earth’s horizon. Yet this joy comes to a halt when faced with the possibility of never coming home or seeing loved ones again.
Our system tries to solve precisely this problem while making use of the resources assigned to the mission. Rather than aborting after a failure, our lunar landing site tool identifies safer alternative locations before the last safe diversion point. These remain similar to the initial site in terms of mission interests, such as minerals and ice, while ensuring sufficient fuel for landing and returning to Earth.Focused on the Moon’s south pole, the program evaluates gradient, luminosity, terrain smoothness, mineral abundance, Earth communication windows, latitude, and longitude using topographic maps. Users explore a 3D model of the Moon, Earth, and Sun, click landmarks or locations to view their characteristics, and compare sites ranked with explanations.A “vicinity” feature displays alternative landing sites within 1.5 km of the location. A calendar and time bar show illumination and Earth visibility, while color-coded overlays highlight terrain and resources. Our goal is prioritizing astronauts’ safety without compromising mission success.
details: When being presented with the opportunity of becoming an astronaut, the excitement that you feel in those moments is unmatched. Nothing can compare to the moment you are officially freed from the boundaries of earth’s horizon and everything that you’ve ever known. But this joy always comes to a halt when being faced with the possibility of never coming home, something all astronauts struggle with and that will always stay on the back of their mind. When picturing their families, the delight is much shorter lived. In spite of all the greatness and meaningfulness this kind of opportunity comes with, they don’t only have to think about, but also accept the fact that it could be the last time they see their loved one.Our system tries to solve precisely this problem, while still having the company make use of all the resources they assigned to the mission. In the past, the best way to prioritize the astronauts’ life in case of failure was to abort the mission, an automatic command that every system comes with built in to make sure human safety is not compromised. Our program allows for both the safety of the humans on board and the success of the mission to be highlighted by calculating, based on the last moment it is possible to change the landing location, a site that is both favorable for safety landing and that is similar enough to the initial location in terms of the mission’s interests (observing minerals and ice, etc.) while also making sure that the fuel reserve is sufficient for landing and returning back to earth. The website finds and displays all reachable locations within a certain radius based on the initial conditions and the last point the ship can safely reach a new optimal landing spot.Our project is a tool that identifies and logs suitable lunar landing locations for specific missions, based on parameters the user enters. The program primarily focuses on the Moon’s south pole, where interest in landing missions is growing. The user can search by a range of parameters: gradient (slope), luminosity (sun visibility), terrain, terrain smoothness, estimated location on the south pole, mineral-rich areas, optimal Earth transmission period, recommended orbit, latitude, and longitude. To evaluate these, the program uses topographic maps preloaded into the software, and users can add more of their own.The interface centers on a zoom-in/zoom-out 3D model of the Moon, Earth, and Sun, including their orbits. A “show landmarks” button displays the landing locations of past Apollo missions, future CLPS mission targets, targets of other commercial lunar missions, and landing sites from other countries’ lunar programs. Clicking any landmark shows all the characteristics listed above. The user can also click anywhere on the Moon and see those same characteristics for that point.Beyond browsing, the program helps users choose a site. The user enters the parameters they want for a landing location, and the program calculates and shows the best option. Once a site is selected, a “vicinity” button shows other candidate landing sites within a 1.5 km radius that have similar characteristics to the selected site. These are ranked from best to worst, with explanations, so the spacecraft can be prepared for a failure that causes it to deviate to another site. Users can also click two or more points on the Moon, and the program compares them from best to worst based on the user’s wanted characteristics, explaining the reasons behind the ranking.At the bottom of the page, a calendar and time bar is always visible. The user picks a calendar date and time for the mission, and the program shows the luminosity, sunset, earthset, and optimal Earth transmission period for that moment. Finally, parameters can be shown as color-coded topographic map overlays, for example the abundance of a certain mineral or of water on the lunar surface, which makes patterns across the terrain easy to see at a glance.From a marketing perspective, Apollo 13 showed that people care more about human stories than achievements. Audiences drifted away after Apollo 11, and the networks barely covered Apollo 13 until an oxygen tank exploded and three lives were at risk. Only then did the world tune in. This matters because public interest plays a big role in whether missions are funded. Engagement comes from people to root for a real loss or a real win, and that engagement keeps missions feasible. This is why observer perspective and crew safety are so important to lunar missions.
